title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
directAnswer: The maximum depth is the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path. The one-line recursive answer: depth = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)), with an empty tree contributing 0. That's postorder DFS — a node's answer depends on its children. The iterative alternative is a BFS that counts how many levels the queue processes. Both are O(n) time; DFS is O(h) space, BFS is O(w) space.

remember.pattern: Postorder DFS aggregation (1 + max of children) — or BFS level counting
rules: Empty tree → depth **0**; a single node → depth **1**. Anchor on these two base values.
It's **postorder**: a node can't know its depth until both children report theirs — children before parent.
Take the **max** of the two child depths, then **+1** for the current node.
BFS alternative: increment a counter once per *level* (drain the whole queue before counting the next).
Depth = node count on the longest path here (LeetCode counts nodes, not edges).
whenToUse: You need the height/depth of a tree or longest root-to-leaf path
Any value where a node's answer is built from its children's answers (bottom-up)
A building block for Balanced Tree, Diameter, and Max Path Sum
antiSignals: You need the MINIMUM depth → BFS short-circuits at the first leaf; DFS must guard one-child nodes
You need per-level node lists → that's Level Order Traversal, not just a count
You need the path itself, not its length → carry the path, not just the count
remember.takeaway: Maximum Depth is the cleanest example of bottom-up (postorder) aggregation: each node returns 1 plus the larger of its children's returns. Internalize this shape — Balanced Tree, Diameter, and Max Path Sum are all this same recursion with a tiny twist.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize tree height as a postorder aggregation — children compute first, parent combines — and can also express it as a level-counting BFS.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Returning 0 for a single node (confusing node-count depth with edge-count height), or using min instead of max, or counting per node instead of per level in the BFS.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State that this is postorder/bottom-up, contrast depth-as-nodes vs height-as-edges, and offer the BFS level count as the iterative variant — then note this is the engine behind Balanced Tree and Diameter.

problemStatement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree, return its **maximum depth**.

A binary tree's maximum depth is the number of nodes along the longest path from the root node down to the farthest leaf node.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 10⁴]
understanding: Find the length (in nodes) of the longest root-to-leaf path. Equivalently, the tree's height + 1 if you count height in edges. We don't need the path itself, just its length, so a single integer flows up the recursion.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is depth measured in nodes or edges?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: LeetCode 104 counts nodes — a single node has depth 1. If the definition were edges, a single node would be depth 0. Confirm which, since it shifts every answer by one.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the tree be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — node count can be 0, and the depth of an empty tree is 0. That's the recursion's base case.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could the tree be deep enough to overflow recursion?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: With up to 10⁴ nodes a skewed tree is 10⁴ deep — usually fine in Java/Python, but mention the BFS alternative if call-stack limits are a concern.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want max or min depth?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Max here. Min depth (LeetCode 111) is subtly different — BFS short-circuits at the first leaf, and DFS must avoid counting through a missing child.

examples.explanation: Longest path is 3 → 20 → 15 (or 3 → 20 → 7), three nodes deep.
Path 1 → 2 has two nodes. The missing left child contributes depth 0.
Empty tree has depth 0 — the base case.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: DFS is the canonical one-liner; BFS level-counting is the iterative equivalent and the natural choice for minimum depth.

approaches.name: Recursive DFS — 1 + max(left, right) (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Start here. It's a one-liner and the textbook example of postorder bottom-up aggregation.
hints: If you somehow knew the depth of the left subtree and the depth of the right subtree, how would you compute the depth of the whole tree?
The tree's depth is 1 (for the root) plus the deeper of its two subtrees. That's a recursive definition — what's the base case?
Base case: a null node has depth 0. Recursive case: return 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Every node is visited exactly once and does O(1) work (a max and an add) → O(n) time. The recursion depth equals the tree height h → O(h) space: O(log n) for a balanced tree, O(n) for a skewed one.
approaches.explanation:
Depth has a naturally recursive definition: the depth of a tree is one more than the depth of its deeper subtree. That single sentence is the whole algorithm.

**Base case.** A null node represents an empty subtree, which has depth 0. Returning 0 here is what makes a leaf node (whose two children are null) report `1 + max(0, 0) = 1` — exactly the node-counting definition.

**Recursive case.** For a real node, ask both children for their depths, take the larger (the longest path goes through whichever subtree is deeper), and add 1 to account for the current node sitting above them. The `max` is essential: a node's depth is dictated by its *deepest* descendant, not the average or the sum.

**Why this is postorder.** A node cannot compute its own depth until *both* children have reported theirs — the work happens on the way back *up* the recursion. That's the definition of postorder / bottom-up processing, and recognizing it is the transferable skill: Balanced Tree, Diameter of a Binary Tree, and Maximum Path Sum all use this same 'children return a value, parent combines it' structure.

**Nodes vs edges.** LeetCode counts depth in nodes, so a single node is depth 1 and an empty tree is depth 0. Some textbooks define height in edges (single node = 0). The code is the same; just confirm the convention so you're not off by one.
approaches.insight: The recursion returns *up* the tree, not down. Each node waits for its children's answers, then folds them with `1 + max(...)`. When you see 'a node's result depends on its subtrees', reach for this postorder shape — it's the most reused tree pattern in interviews.

dryRun.intro: Postorder: leaves resolve first, then parents combine. Depth returned shown per node.

code.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def maxDepth(self, root: TreeNode) -> int:
    if not root:                                        # empty subtree
        return 0
    return 1 + max(self.maxDepth(root.left),            # parent combines
                   self.maxDepth(root.right))           # children report first

java.explanation: Base case — an empty subtree contributes zero depth, making a leaf evaluate to 1.
Children must finish before the parent — this is the postorder ordering.
Longest path goes through the DEEPER child; +1 counts the current node.

python.explanation: max picks the deeper subtree; +1 accounts for this node. Both recursions resolve before the add.

diagrams.title: Depths bubbling up [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]
diagrams.caption: Leaves return 1; node 20 returns 2; root 3 returns 1 + max(1,2) = 3.

edgeCases.behavior: 1 + max(0,0) = 1 — a single node has depth 1 under the node-counting definition.
Each level adds 1 down the left spine → returns 4; recursion depth is also 4 (O(n)).

pitfalls: Returning 0 for a single node — that's the edge-count height, not the node-count depth LeetCode wants.
Using min instead of max — gives the shortest path, not the longest.
Adding the two child depths instead of taking the max — that's not a path length at all.

approaches.name: Iterative BFS — Count the Levels
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as the iterative version, especially if the interviewer worries about recursion depth or pivots toward minimum depth (where BFS shines).
hints: Depth equals the number of levels in the tree. How would you process a tree one full level at a time?
Use a queue. At the start of each outer loop, the queue holds exactly one level; drain all of them while enqueuing their children.
Increment a depth counter once per level (per drain), not once per node. When the queue empties, the counter is the depth.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is enqueued and dequeued once → O(n) time. The queue holds at most one level at a time, so its size is bounded by the tree's maximum width w → O(w) space (up to O(n) for the widest level of a balanced tree).
approaches.explanation:
Maximum depth is just the number of levels, so a level-order BFS that counts levels answers it directly without recursion.

**The level-drain trick.** Seed a queue with the root and a depth counter at 0. Each outer-loop iteration represents one level: record the current queue size (that's how many nodes are on this level), then dequeue *exactly that many* nodes, enqueuing each one's children. After draining the level, increment the depth. When the queue is empty, every level has been counted and the depth is the answer.

**Why record the size up front.** The queue grows as you enqueue children, so you must snapshot `levelSize` before the inner loop — otherwise you'd bleed into the next level and miscount. This 'capture the size, then loop exactly that many times' idiom is the universal BFS-by-level pattern, reused in Level Order Traversal, Right Side View, and Zigzag Traversal.

**When BFS beats DFS.** For *maximum* depth they're equivalent. But for *minimum* depth (LeetCode 111), BFS is strictly better: the first leaf you encounter is on the shallowest level, so you can return immediately instead of exploring the whole tree. Mentioning that distinction shows you understand *why* you'd pick one traversal over the other, not just that both exist.
approaches.insight: The 'snapshot the queue size, then dequeue exactly that many' move is the heart of every level-by-level BFS. Counting levels with it gives depth; collecting the popped values per level gives Level Order Traversal — same skeleton, different payload.

dryRun.intro: Each outer iteration drains one full level and bumps depth. Queue shown front-first.

java.explanation: Snapshot BEFORE the inner loop — children enqueued below would otherwise inflate the count.
Process exactly one level's worth of nodes.
Enqueue children for the next level; skip nulls.
Increment once per LEVEL, not per node — that's what makes the count equal the depth.

python.explanation: len(queue) is captured at loop start, fixing the level boundary.
One increment per fully drained level.

edgeCases.behavior: Guard returns 0 before the queue starts.
Queue peaks at the last level (~n/2 nodes) → O(n) space worst case for BFS.

pitfalls: Reading queue.size() inside the inner loop instead of snapshotting it — bleeds levels together.
Incrementing depth per node instead of per level — wildly overcounts.
Enqueuing null children — can cause a null dereference when you later poll them.

commonMistakes: Returning 0 for a single node (edge-count height vs node-count depth confusion).
Using min instead of max, yielding the shortest path.
In the BFS version, incrementing the counter per node instead of per level.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: min instead of max
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Maximum depth follows the LONGEST root-to-leaf path. Using min returns the shortest path length, which is a different problem (and even that needs a one-child guard).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Counting per node instead of per level in BFS
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Incrementing the depth on every dequeue counts nodes, not levels. You must snapshot the level size and bump depth once per drained level.

followupVariations.title: Minimum Depth of Binary Tree
followupVariations.hint: BFS returns at the first leaf; in DFS, a node with one missing child must take the existing child's depth, not min with 0.

followupVariations.title: Balanced Binary Tree
followupVariations.hint: Same height recursion, but also check |leftHeight - rightHeight| ≤ 1 at every node.

followupVariations.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
followupVariations.hint: Track leftDepth + rightDepth at each node while the recursion returns the height upward.

followupVariations.title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
followupVariations.hint: Same level-drain BFS, but collect the popped values per level instead of just counting.

patternNote: Postorder (bottom-up) aggregation: children return a value, the parent combines them with 1 + max(...). This is the most reused tree recursion — Balanced Tree, Diameter, and Max Path Sum are all the same shape with extra bookkeeping. The BFS level-count is the iterative twin and the gateway to all level-order problems.
